slides.0.title: Classification: PDO, PGI and Traditional Terms
slides.0.subtitle: The legal framework and ageing labels
slides.1.title: PDO and PGI: two tiers
slides.1.highlights.0.title: PDO (Protected Designation of Origin)
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Grapes must be 100% from the zone and the wine produced and bottled there; 33 are registered
slides.1.highlights.1.title: PGI (Protected Geographical Indication)
slides.1.highlights.1.content: At least 85% of grapes from the zone, the rest from elsewhere in Greece; about 114 are registered
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Three levels of PGI
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Regional (8 zones), District (37, broadly by prefecture) and Area (smaller zones)
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Grape flexibility
slides.1.highlights.3.content: PGIs may use native and international grapes (e.g. Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah) as each zone's rules allow
slides.1.content: The key differences are sourcing (100% vs 85%) and strictness. Note: some sources cite "80%"; EU rules and most teaching materials use 85%, so confirm against official documents before citing.
slides.2.title: Old versus new terms
slides.2.highlights.0.title: OPAP
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Appellation of Origin of Superior Quality, for dry wines; a red neck band
slides.2.highlights.1.title: OPE
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Controlled Appellation of Origin, for sweet and fortified wines; a blue neck band
slides.2.highlights.2.title: How the system evolved
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Both date from 1969 legislation and have sat under the EU PDO framework since 2009; producers may still use the Greek terms on labels
slides.2.highlights.3.title: A mnemonic
slides.2.highlights.3.content: OPAP + OPE = PDO; the other geographic wines fall under PGI
slides.2.content: Seeing an old term tells you at once that it maps to PDO, and whether it is dry or sweet/fortified.
slides.3.title: Traditional terms: Retsina and Verdea
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Retsina
slides.3.highlights.0.content: An EU Traditional Appellation reserved for Greece; Aleppo pine (Pinus halepensis) resin is added during fermentation and removed afterwards
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Resin limits
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Sources cite a cap of about 1% by volume (10 g/L), added before fermentation is two-thirds complete
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Verdea
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Regional PGIs
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Retsina also carries many geographical indications (mainly in Attica, Boeotia and Euboea)
slides.3.content: A Traditional term is a style identity on the label and can coexist with a geographical indication (PDO/PGI).
slides.4.title: Reserve and Grand Reserve
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Where it applies
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Only for PDO wines from former OPAP/OPE zones; PGIs cannot use them
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Total ageing (common course figures)
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Reserve: white 2 years, red 3 years; Grand Reserve: white 3 years, red 4 years
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Oak and bottle breakdown
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Court of Master Sommeliers materials list: Reserve 6 months oak + 6 months bottle; Grand Reserve 1 + 1 year (white) and 2 + 2 years (red)
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Verification note
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Breakdowns differ slightly between sources and each PDO also has its own rules (e.g. Mavrodaphne of Patras); use the official product specification before exams or citations
slides.4.content: This lesson asks for the concept and scope only; the month-by-month detail is a verification exercise in Level 3 (Regulation in Depth).
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
What share of grapes must a PGI wine generally take from the named zone?
PGI requires at least 85%; PDO requires 100%.
Which old term covered sweet and fortified wines, with a blue neck band?
OPAP was for dry wines (red band); OPE for sweet and fortified wines (blue band).
Which wines may use the Reserve and Grand Reserve terms?
B. PDO wines from former OPAP/OPE zones
A rules-concept question: PGIs cannot use them.
A. An EU Traditional Appellation reserved for Greece
It is a style identity running alongside PDO/PGI.
